title: Top chipmakers embrace ASML’s $400M machines, agree to crucial chipmaking change
gist: Samsung and TSMC will adopt ASML's $400M high-NA EUV lithography machines (Samsung for memory by 2028, TSMC for leading-edge logic by 2030), and along with Intel they are shifting the industry's photomask standard from 6-inch to 12-inch, a change ASML's CTO says could boost high-NA EUV productivity by 40 percent — all while China remains locked out of EUV technology and reportedly 15 years from a homegrown equivalent.

themes.theme: Industry-wide adoption of high-NA EUV and a coordinated standards shift

insights.claim: Samsung Electronics and TSMC announced plans to adopt ASML's high-NA EUV lithography machines, joining Intel, which has already been using the technology since July 2026 for high-volume manufacturing of Panther Lake mobile processors.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Confirms Intel currently holds a real-world manufacturing lead in deploying next-gen lithography ahead of its two largest foundry rivals, a data point relevant to competitive positioning in the foundry race.
insights.locator: Leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor

insights.claim: Samsung plans to use ASML's high-NA EUV machines to produce memory chips starting in 2028, while TSMC targets 2030 for using the technology to manufacture its most advanced chips for customers including AMD, Apple, Nvidia, and Qualcomm.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Gives investors concrete adoption timelines to track for capex cycles at Samsung and TSMC and to model when their fabless customers (Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm) could access chips built on this next-gen node.
insights.locator: South Korea's Samsung plans to use ASML's high NA EUV

insights.claim: Samsung, TSMC, and Intel are working with ASML to shift the chipmaking photomask standard from 6-inch to 12-inch, a change ASML CTO Marco Pieters said could eventually improve high-NA EUV machine productivity by 40 percent.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 40 percent productivity gain on $400M machines materially changes the economics of leading-edge fabs; tracking consortium progress on the 12-inch photomask standard is a leading indicator for capacity and cost curves in advanced chipmaking.
insights.locator: That shift could eventually improve the chipmaking productivity

insights.claim: SK Hynix is considering joining the industry consortium overseeing the switch to 12-inch photomasks and, like Samsung, is also aiming to start high-NA EUV memory chip production in 2028.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Signals near-industry-wide convergence around the 2028 timeline for high-NA EUV memory production, suggesting the memory chip supply response to today's shortage may not meaningfully accelerate before then.
insights.locator: The South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix

insights.claim: The rush by tech companies to build new AI data centers has contributed to a global memory chip shortage that has driven up prices for smartphones, laptops, and gaming machines, making improved chip production a business imperative as the AI investment cycle continues.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Directly links AI capex to consumer electronics inflation via memory chip scarcity — an inflationary transmission channel from AI infrastructure buildout into everyday device prices worth monitoring for consumer hardware margins and CPI-adjacent effects.
insights.locator: Improved production of chips has become a business imperative

insights.claim: ASML still supplies Chinese companies like SMIC with older-generation deep-ultraviolet lithography machines but has been blocked from exporting most of its advanced chipmaking machines to China under Dutch government restrictions and US political pressure.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Confirms the export control chokepoint remains intact and is the key structural constraint keeping Chinese chipmakers behind on leading-edge nodes, a factor central to any China semiconductor self-sufficiency thesis.

insights.claim: Despite unproven US government allegations that China managed to obtain one of ASML's EUV lithography machines, Chinese companies face an uphill battle building a homegrown EUV supply chain, with a Zeiss Group executive predicting China would need 15 years to develop EUV lithography machines domestically.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 15-year estimate from ASML's exclusive optics supplier gives a concrete (if contested) timeline anchor for when China could close the EUV gap — useful for scenario-testing semiconductor decoupling and China tech self-sufficiency investment theses.
insights.locator: An executive at Germany's Zeiss Group

insights.claim: ASML's high-NA EUV machines generate light by continually zapping molten tin into plasma at temperatures around 200,000°C, then use mirrors to collect and redirect that light into a bus-size lithography tool that projects circuitry patterns onto silicon wafers, with the newest high-NA machines using bigger mirrors and an improved optical system for more precise focus.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Illustrates the extreme engineering complexity and cost basis behind $400M machines, explaining why ASML retains a near-total monopoly on this manufacturing step and why replicating it (e.g., by China) is so difficult.
insights.locator: This has necessitated development of an incredibly complex system
